# Entity Interpolation

Snapshots arrive at the tick rate and at the mercy of the network; frames render at whatever the
monitor does. Drawing remote players at the last received position gives visible stepping. Entity
interpolation fixes this by **rendering remote entities deliberately in the past**, between two
snapshots that have both already arrived.

The cost is a fixed, chosen latency on everyone else's position. The benefit is that motion is always
smooth, because you are interpolating between two known points rather than extrapolating past one.

## The four parameters that matter

[[stickfps]]'s `RemotePlayerInterpolator` is a compact reference implementation:

- **Buffer depth: 2 snapshots per remote player.** The minimum for interpolation — one behind, one
  ahead. Deeper buffers absorb more jitter at more latency.
- **Render delay: 100 ms.** Remote players are drawn 100 ms behind the newest snapshot, so a late
  packet within that window costs nothing.
- **Shortest-arc angle blending.** Yaw is blended with `lerpAngle`, not a linear lerp.
- **Staleness cutoff: 1000 ms.** A player with no snapshot for a second is removed rather than held.
  Leavers **vanish instead of freezing** — a small decision that changes how the game reads, because
  a frozen avatar is indistinguishable from a stationary opponent.

## The ±π seam

Naive interpolation of an angle is wrong exactly once per rotation. Yaw wraps at ±π, so blending
from `+3.10` to `-3.10` takes the long way round: remote players in [[stickfps]] were observed
**spinning a full 360°** whenever an opponent crossed the seam. `lerpAngle` picks the shortest arc
by normalising the difference into (−π, π] before blending.

This is the canonical bug of the technique. Any interpolated quantity with a wrap point — heading,
hue, time of day — has the same failure, and it is invisible in testing until something crosses the
seam.

## Why it is not prediction

[[client-side-prediction-and-reconciliation]] runs the *local* player ahead of the server so input
feels instant. Interpolation runs *remote* players behind it so motion looks smooth. The two point in
opposite directions on purpose, and the gap between them is the latency budget you are actually
shooting through — which matters because [[server-authoritative-netcode]] here has no lag
compensation, so the server judges hits against current positions, not the interpolated positions the
shooter saw.

The alternative to interpolating is **extrapolation** (dead reckoning): keep moving the entity along
its last velocity when snapshots stop. It removes the delay but invents positions, so it produces
snap-backs when the guess is wrong. [[stickfps]] does not extrapolate.
